subject: Coffee & Tea
title: How Black Tea Is Made
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How Black Tea Is Made.

hook.text: Black tea is green tea that's been fully oxidized. The process turns pale leaves dark and transforms flavor.

buildup.text: Leaves are withered, rolled to break cell walls, then spread on trays to oxidize for 2–4 hours.

discovery.text: During oxidation, catechins convert to theaflavins (brisk) and thearubigins (body and color).

twist.text: Heat is applied to stop oxidation at the right moment. Too early makes it taste green; too late makes it flat.

climax.text: Black tea is the world's most consumed type, accounting for about 78% of all tea produced globally.

punchline.text: Full oxidation, full body. Black tea conquered the world.

quiz.question: What percentage of global tea production is black tea?

details.summary: Black tea production involves withering, rolling, full oxidation, and drying. After picking, leaves are spread to wilt and lose moisture, then rolled to break cell walls and trigger oxidation. Leaves darken fully over hours before final drying locks in bold, malty, and sometimes fruity flavors.
details.whyItMatters: Black tea is the world's most consumed tea type. Understanding its production explains the rich, robust flavors that make it the global default.
takeaways: Leaves are fully oxidized during black tea production
Rolling breaks cell walls to initiate oxidation
Final drying halts oxidation and preserves flavor

faq.question: How long does black tea oxidation take?
faq.answer: Full oxidation typically takes two to four hours in controlled rooms at 25 to 30 degrees Celsius with high humidity. The tea master judges readiness by color, aroma, and feel. Under-oxidation produces a harsh taste, while over-oxidation yields flat, dull flavors.

faq.question: What is CTC black tea versus orthodox?
faq.answer: CTC stands for crush, tear, curl, a mechanized process that produces tiny, uniform granules for tea bags. Orthodox production uses traditional rolling that preserves whole leaves. CTC brews fast and strong; orthodox teas offer more nuance and complexity but take longer to steep.
